item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=experimental+measurements+of+stochasticity+and+mutation+rates+in+protocell+compositional+inheritance&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6249639\", \"title\": [\"Variance-dependent inheritance drives symmetry breaking in a protocell model\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Symmetry breaking in prebiotic and protocellular systems is typically attributed to fitness gradients, catalytic amplification, or explicit selective advantages. The possibility that stochastic variance alone can generate macroscopic asymmetry in strictly symmetric populations remains insufficiently explored. The present study tests whether direction-neutral, variance-dependent mechanisms can induce residence-time symmetry breaking in finite protocell populations without fitness differences or absorbing states. Two paired-noise stochastic models are analyzed. Model A implements a Moran birth–death process in which reproduction probability depends on a symmetric internal-variance proxy. Model B combines threshold-triggered division with composition-dependent partition noise, such that inheritance fidelity varies symmetrically with internal composition. In both models, symmetry breaking is quantified using a pre-registered neutral-quantile threshold, defined as the 0.99 quantile of the neutral symmetry-distance distribution after burn-in, thereby fixing the expected false-positive rate at 1\\\\%. The Variance-dependent reproduction rate (Model A) produces small or negligible and parameter-sensitive increases in tail occupancy. In contrast, variance-dependent partition noise under threshold division (Model B) generates strong and monotonic residence-time bias, with large effect sizes and highly significant paired statistical tests. Neutral-equivalence sanity checks confirm exact matching under zero coupling, validating the paired-noise implementation. These results demonstrate that stabilization of inherited state, rather than mean fitness advantage can produce macroscopic occupancy dominance in symmetric stochastic populations. Variance-mediated amplification therefore provides a plausible and general mechanism for symmetry breaking in protocell systems and other nonequilibrium stochastic populations.</jats…
